Chapter 7: The Night of Broken Glass—A City Shattered.
There are moments in life when history bursts through the everyday, changing everything in just a single night. For this family, that moment arrived with the sharp, chilling sound of glass breaking in the streets below. Suddenly, the city was swept up in a storm of violence—shops were looted, synagogues set on fire, and families forced out of the homes they'd always known.
The regime tried to call it a “spontaneous outburst,” but deep down, everyone understood it was anything but random. It was planned.
The ambassador’s daughter stood at her window, watching as flames flickered and rose in the distance. She saw neighbors—people she’d grown up waving to—now huddling in doorways, their faces drawn and pale with fear. When morning finally came, the streets were covered in broken glass, and the air was thick with the heavy smell of smoke and loss. For the city’s Jewish community, who’d already endured years of discrimination, this was something far worse. Now, terror was out in the open.
The ambassador walked through the aftermath, his heart weighed down by what he saw. He listened to survivors, heard their stories, and tried to offer whatever comfort he could. But in moments like these, words just weren’t enough. So, he sent urgent reports back to Washington, describing every detail, pleading for action—yet the world, once again, seemed to look the other way.
For the family, that night changed everything. The daughter—who’d always believed friendship could cross any divide—now saw how quickly fear could turn friends into strangers. And the ambassador, who’d tried so hard to make a difference within the system, realized that quiet diplomacy no longer had a place here. The city they once loved had vanished, replaced by something colder and full of danger.
In the days that followed, the family made a choice. They opened their home to anyone in need—offering food, shelter, and, maybe most important, a listening ear. They knew they couldn’t change the course of history, but they could decide how they’d respond. In the face of cruelty, they chose compassion.
